name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Assign the Content Strategy Lead to enforce a single, shared Decision Ledger for all cross-department creative projects. This eliminates duplicate debates and keeps every team aligned on the same priorities. The trade-off is slower initial adoption if some teams resist centralization, but the long-term clarity outweighs the friction.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The Decision Ledger centralizes control but risks turning the Content Strategy Lead into a bottleneck—what happens when a team’s urgent creative need stalls waiting for a single sign-off? A better fix is to give every department a lightweight veto slot on the Ledger, not full ownership; settle it by measuring how often the veto blocks progress versus how often it prevents misalignment.

name: Chisel
text:
Assign the Content Strategy Lead to own the Decision Ledger and enforce a *time-boxed veto window* for departments. This keeps one clear owner for alignment while giving teams a fast way to flag blockers without derailing the process. The trade-off is that vetoes must be rare and justified—otherwise the Ledger becomes a negotiation forum, not a decision tool.

name: Sift
text: The time-boxed veto lets teams game the system by forcing the Lead into a binary choice: accept the veto or delay the project. Instead, require vetoes to cite a *specific, documented conflict* with the project’s stated goals—no vague objections. Settle it by piloting the rule for one sprint and measuring how often vetoes are overturned.

name: Scope
text: Assign the Content Strategy Lead to pilot a *single, shared Decision Ledger* for all cross-department creative projects, with a strict 48-hour veto window per department. This forces alignment by making priorities visible and decisions traceable, cutting duplicate debates. The trade-off is slower initial buy-in if teams resist centralization, but the long-term clarity outweighs the friction.

name: Scriv
text: The 48-hour veto window turns the Content Strategy Lead into a referee in a game where the rules keep changing—departments will exploit the window to renegotiate priorities mid-sprint. Instead, give every team a *one-time, non-renewable veto credit* per quarter tied to a documented, irreversible conflict with the project’s stated goals; this forces them to choose when to burn political capital. Settle it by tracking veto usage and project velocity over two quarters—if vetoes spike or projects stall, the rule dies.

name: Reel
text: Assign the Content Strategy Lead to own a single, shared Decision Ledger with a *one-time, non-renewable veto credit per department per quarter*—no extensions, no renegotiations. This forces teams to commit to decisions upfront while giving them a last-resort escape hatch for truly irreversible conflicts. The trade-off is that some urgent needs may stall for a quarter, but the system prevents constant mid-sprint derailments and keeps priorities stable.

name: Scriv
text: The one-time veto credit per quarter is a gimmick that ignores how creative work actually stalls—teams will hoard vetoes for minor gripes, then unleash them when a project finally matters, turning the Ledger into a ticking time bomb. Instead, tie vetoes to *clear, measurable project risks* (e.g., legal exposure, brand misalignment) and let the Content Strategy Lead audit them retroactively; settle it by tracking veto usage against project delays for one full quarter.
